extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of humor; general readers
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic survey summarizing major theoretical accounts of what makes things humorous (relief, superiority, incongruity, benign-violation, linguistic/script theories, evolutionary and cognitive accounts, etc.), with examples and key variants. Useful for readers seeking conceptual criteria for when and why humor occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is a mechanism for pent-up emotions or tension through emotional relief; laughter serves as a homeostatic mechanism reducing psychological stress and releasing excess nervous/psychic energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains laughter as release of tension (tickling, anticipation/relief patterns). Includes historical proponents (Herbert Spencer, Freud, Kant) and applied notions such as comic relief in drama. Notes tendentious vs non-tendentious humor (Freud): tendentious uses victimization/hostility masked by innocuous jokework. Empirical studies (e.g., Zillmann & Bryant) support interaction of innocuous cues and victimization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor arises from feeling superior to others; people laugh at the misfortunes, infirmities, or past failings of others because it creates a sense of glory or superiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roots in Plato, Aristotle, Hobbes (laughter as 'sudden glory'). Hobbes lists typical triggers (unexpected personal success, perception of defects/infirmities, conceiving absurdity abstracted from persons). Notes interplay with aggression and hostility; also that some writers treat it prescriptively (punching up/down). Article records criticisms that many humour types are not reducible to superiority and affective responses are distinct from humor itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affective disposition theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience moral judgments and dispositions toward characters determine amusement: people enjoy good things happening to good people and bad things to bad people; disposition toward actor and victor modulates mirth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides quantitative-style guidelines: greater negative disposition toward disparaged agent increases mirth; greater positive disposition toward disparaged agent decreases mirth; similar rules for disposition toward victor. Explains audience variation, and why some disparagements fail to amuse (e.g., tragedy evokes pity instead). Connects to ethical discussion of punching up vs punching down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity theory (incongruous juxtaposition / incongruity-resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor and laughter rely on incongruity—anything contrary to expectation—often resolved by a punchline that causes a cognitive shift or reinterpretation (incongruity-resolution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains linguistic examples and riddle jokes (e.g., 'black and white and read all over' -> newspaper). Historical proponents include Hutcheson, Beattie, Kant, Schopenhauer. Key elements: surprise, cognitive dissonance, sudden shift of perspective. Variants emphasize single clash, assemblage, or shift/resolution. Bergson, Latta, Boyd, Koestler offer modifications (e.g., frame collision, structure-mapping). Notes that incongruity often pairs with relief or superiority elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign Violation Theory (BVT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor occurs when (1) something threatens one's sense of how the world 'ought to be,' (2) the threatening situation seems benign, and (3) a person perceives both interpretations simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developed by McGraw & Warren (building on Tom Veatch). Examples: play fighting, tickling, moral norm violations that are psychologically distant or occur within competing norms. Empirically tested contexts: moral violations perceived as benign when observer is less committed to the violated norm (e.g., non-churchgoers amused by church raffle story). Emphasizes context and individual differences: violation must be both recognizably wrong and simultaneously construed as safe/acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script-based Semantic Theory of Humor (SSTH)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal jokes evoke humor when the text is compatible with two different semantic 'scripts' and those scripts are opposite or incompatible; the punchline triggers an abrupt switch from the primary to the secondary script.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raskin's formal linguistic account is strictly verbal: two conditions: (i) compatibility with two semantic scripts, (ii) the scripts are opposite. Provides script-opposition categories (actual/non-actual, normal/abnormal, possible/impossible, good/bad, life/death, obscene/non-obscene, etc.). Example: 'Is the doctor at home?' joke (DOCTOR vs LOVER scripts). Cultural dependence of script inventories noted; must establish a clever connection (not mere juxtaposition).

rubrics_metrics.name: General Theory of Verbal Humor (GTVH) / Knowledge Resources (KRs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal jokes can be modeled by six independent Knowledge Resources that determine joke structure and similarity: Script Opposition (SO), Logical Mechanism (LM), Situation (SI), Target (TA), Narrative Strategy (NS), and Language (LA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GTVH integrates SSTH (SO) and adds: LM (mechanism linking scripts, e.g., pun, faulty logic), SI (objects/props), TA (butt/target of joke), NS (narrative format: narrative/dialogue/riddle), LA (exact wording/functional elements). KRs are hierarchical (upper KRs constrain lower ones). Use: modeling joke variants and measuring joke similarity (examples: light bulb joke variants). NS expansion allows analysis beyond short jokes to humorous texts of any length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer model of humor (Suslov)
rubrics_metrics.description: A computational/biological model treating humor as an information-processing malfunction: a false version is quickly deleted from consciousness (incongruity-resolution) with timing playing a crucial role; biological function is efficient transmission of processed information and neural energy dynamics produce laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adds timing to ambiguity-based accounts; maps deletion of false interpretations to neural zeroing and motor cortex activation (laughter). Claims humor emerges naturally in biological systems and explains individual differences, role of intonation, nervous laughter, and absence of humor from trite jokes. Notes practical realization needs extensive databases and neural-network implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misattribution theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences sometimes cannot identify precisely what they find funny and misattribute their amusement to innocent elements, while the true cause may be tendentious/taboo/hostility elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originated from Zillmann & Bryant (1980) with Freud antecedents; explains how taboo/hostility produce laughter while audiences report laughing at innocuous features. Useful for explaining laughs at victimization masked by jokework and transferred excitation effects in experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontic-epistemic theory of humor (Marteinson)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is a reaction to a cognitive impasse where Social Being appears no longer real; comic perception arises when factual reality conflicts with normative/social reality (Deculturation or Relativisation), momentarily disabling social perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posits laughter resets social perception by anesthetizing the mind with euphoria and allowing forgetting of the comic stimulus. Connects to Bergson's ideas about social reality vs factual reality; emphasizes epistemological/rebooting function of laughter rather than mere affective release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual selection / evolutionary signaling (Geoffrey Miller)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor evolved by sexual selection as an indicator of desirable traits (e.g., intelligence); humor signaled fitness to potential mates rather than direct survival advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues humor had little direct survival value in early hominids; instead it functioned as mate attraction, indicating cognitive traits. Presented as an evolutionary account explaining display of humor in courtship contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection-of-mistaken-reasoning / cognitive error-detection theory (Hurley, Dennett, Adams)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor evolved because it strengthens the brain's ability to detect mistakes in active belief structures; humor aids finding mistaken reasoning and thus enhances problem-solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents humor as adaptive for practical cognition: identifying false or inconsistent representations. Links to sexual selection insofar as the capacity to spot errors signals intelligence; uses analyses of jokes to show how humor exercises error-detection mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as a defense mechanism (Vaillant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is an adaptive psychological defense (level 4) that allows overt expression of unpleasant ideas/feelings in a way that gives pleasure to others and helps cope with distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes humor (overt, pleasure-giving) from wit (displacement). Used in psychodynamic frameworks to classify ways individuals manage distress. Useful when evaluating therapeutic or interpersonal functions of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense-of-humor vs sense-of-seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful humor requires both a sense of humor and a sense of seriousness to signal when something is not to be taken literally; misreading this balance can lead to 'bad taste' where humor crosses into unintended seriousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights pragmatic competence: when humor communicates serious points (court jesters) or when bad taste causes offense. Evaluative criterion for whether humor achieves intended framing and audience uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor, metonymy, and allegory in humor (computational/cognitive approaches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor, metonymy, conceptual blending and structure-mapping are central mechanisms in many forms of linguistic and literary humor, enabling novel mappings and unexpected interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tony Veale's computational approach draws on Gentner's structure-mapping, Lakoff & Johnson's conceptual metaphor, Turner & Fauconnier's conceptual blending. Bakhtin's poetic metaphor and allegory perspectives also applied. Useful for analyzing humor that depends on figurative language and complex semantic mapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: O'Shannon model of the comedic event (Dan O'Shannon)
rubrics_metrics.description: A unified framework with four main sections—context, information, aspects of awareness, and enhancers/inhibitors—where context shapes reception, information contains cognitive incongruity, aspects of awareness determine interpretive vantage, and enhancers/inhibitors (e.g., superiority, relief, identification) modulate response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how low incongruity plus enhancers (superiority, relief) or high incongruity produce different responses (visceral vs appreciative). Elements across sections interact; model accommodates many comedy branches and includes timing, evolutionary notes, and concept of comedic entropy. Use as integrative evaluative framework for comedic events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unnoticed fall-back to former behavior patterns model
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter signals awareness of an unnoticed fall-back to former behaviour patterns; unifies superiority and incongruity elements and links ticklishness via evolutionary posture changes (bipedalism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines laughter as an acoustic signal to alert others to a detected reversion to prior behavior; connects social signalling with cognitive detection of pattern slips. Offers a behavioral/signal interpretation rather than purely cognitive or affective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bergson's theory (mechanism applied to life / rigidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic arises from 'mechanism applied to life': rigidity, inelasticity, or mechanical behavior in living beings produces the comic; laughter performs social/moral functions by condemning ludicrous and eccentric behaviours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes examples like falling, imitation, automatic conventions, absent-mindedness, repetitive gestures; sees laughter as intellectual, detached activity focused on rigidity rather than ugliness. Useful for evaluating physical/comedic situations where automatism contrasts with liveliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex systems / dynamical systems approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply complexity/chaos theory to humor: interacting parts of communicative systems give rise to collective humorous behaviour; change, emergence and interaction with environment are central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invites transdisciplinary research and models for conversational humor, meme propagation, and dynamics of incongruity/resolution. Examples include Tschacher & Haken's dynamics of incongruity-resolution, Demjén's complexity-based models of running jokes in discourse communities.
